newsitem.title: USA: NFL AMERICAN FOOTBALL-PACKERS SENSE THEIR TIME HAS COME - AGAIN.
newsitem.headline: NFL AMERICAN FOOTBALL-PACKERS SENSE THEIR TIME HAS COME - AGAIN.

text.p: Green Bay Packers coach Mike Holmgren said Friday there is a feeling about his team that their time to again be NFL champions has come and they are anxious to get on with the big game.
"I think we were ready to play the game yesterday," Holmgren told reporters just two days before he leads his team against the New England Patriots in Super Bowl XXXI.
"I do sense a feeling that this is our time, this is our game," he said of his Packers, who are 29 years removed from the last Green Bay team to win a Super Bowl.
"But talking about it and wanting it doesn't get it done. You have to go out and perform."
Holmgren, however, has said he is never in danger of getting too confident.

"Any time I start feeling pretty good about myself or what we've accomplished, my daughters or my wife remind me that 'you were 0-22 at one time,'" he said of a particularly bad stretch in his high school coaching days.

On Saturday night Holmgren will reveal to his team the scripted first 15 offensive plays he and his coaches have devised for their opening drives -- a tradition that goes back to his days as an assistant with the San Francisco 49ers.
Holmgren likes to start the game with plays "decided in a calmer, quieter setting."
"Nobody sees them until Saturday night," he said.
He also hopes the script will help keep his brilliant quarterback, Brett Favre, from getting overly excited, as is his habit.
"If he could get more excited for the game than he has been in some games in the past, that would be a little frightening to me," Holmgren said.
"He has a tendency to start off and throw what I affectionately call rocket balls early in the game. They could go anywhere."
Holmgren, a big tedddy bear of a man who appears far less intimidating than many of his NFL peers, said Favre told him "all I need is to get that first big hit and I'll be fine."
"I said, but you're the guy getting hit, you're not hitting someone. Let's do it another way," Holmgren joked.
Although his team is favoured by 14 points, Holmgren referred to himself as "the decided underdog in the coaching comparison."
However, he did not begrudge New England coach Bill Parcells the excessive attention he has received in the run-up to the NFL extravaganza.
"Bill, he's everywhere, newspapers, magazines. He's larger than life. You know, he looks good on television," Holmgren said, chucking.
"It's earned, he's won two Super Bowls (with the New York Giants) and that's special. I'm getting my team ready to play too."
Holmgren has been to two previous Super Bowls with the 49ers -- both victories -- but this is his first trip as a head coach.
"They're all special," he said.
"The first one was unbelievable because it was the first one," he said of Super Bowl XXIII, when he was quarterback coach to the great Joe Montana.
"The second one was unbelievable because I was the (offensive) coordinator and I was calling the plays."
As a head coach, with expanded responsibilities, Holmgren admitted he has not been sleeping nearly as well.
Still, he added, "this is a wonderful, wonderful experience. It's awesome."

Holmgren, who travels to work on Vince Lombardi Avenue and who will be playing for the Lombardi trophy Sunday, seems at peace with the Packers glorious past, rather than haunted by pressure to live up to the coaching legend who won five championships in the 1960s, including the first two Super Bowls.
"I think what the Lombardi era has meant to the league and the Packer organisation should never be put to rest. They will be part of football ... for as long as we play the game," Holmgren said.

"They were special. It's been my privilege since I've been in Green Bay to meet almost everyone of the fellows that are still around that played on those teams. They were the best for a number of years in that particular time and I really respect them.
"But this particular team will also be be recognised as a special team."
